body: The underlying providers have timeouts. Where do you see this?

We are actually seeing the agent wedge in two specific areas that fall *outside* the purview of the underlying LLM provider's timeouts:

**1. Tool Executions (Userspace Hanging)**
The LLM providers do not execute the tools; the agent loop handles `Tool.execute()` directly. If a tool hangs (e.g., a bash command waiting for user input without `stdin`, an infinite loop in a script, or an unresponsive MCP server via stdio), the `execute()` promise never resolves. Because the provider isn't involved during tool execution, its timeouts don't apply, and the agent loop wedges indefinitely waiting for the tool result. 

**2. Stream Iteration (TCP Half-Open/Idle Drops)**
While provider SDKs generally have robust *connection* and *request* timeouts, they often lack *idle read* timeouts during active streaming. If the HTTP stream connects and starts yielding events, but the network silently drops (a TCP half-open connection) or the provider's backend hangs mid-generation without cleanly closing the stream, `iterator.next()` will wait forever. 

This PR enforces a configurable, hard boundary at the `agent-loop` level using `Promise.race()` for both `iterator.next()` and `tool.execute()`. This ensures that no matter what the underlying provider SDK or the executed tool does, the loop is guaranteed to either advance or fail closed on a timeout.
I don't really understand. Do you have a repro?

Hi! Thank you for reviewing this. I'm happy to clarify. 
Yes, my repository where we run into this is here: [https://github.com/Paramveersingh-S/fluffy-harness](https://github.com/Paramveersingh-S/fluffy-harness)
We build enterprise extensions for the Pi agent (like MCP bridges and permission guards). While you are entirely correct that the underlying LLM SDKs (like OpenAI/Anthropic) have their own request timeouts, those timeouts do not cover all the boundaries where the `AgentLoop` can wedge. 
Specifically, we see the agent hang in two distinct areas that fall completely outside the purview of the provider SDKs:
 1. The Userspace Tool Hanging Bug
The LLM provider does not execute the tools; our `AgentLoop` does. When the provider yields a `tool_call`, the HTTP request finishes and the provider's job is technically done. 
Our agent then invokes the tool's `execute()` promise. In our `pi-bridge` extension, if an external MCP server goes unresponsive, the `execute()` promise never resolves. 
- The Result:The `AgentLoop` is permanently stuck waiting on the tool, wedging the application indefinitely.
 2. The TCP Half-Open Streaming Bug
While provider SDKs have *request* timeouts, they rely on native Node.js stream iterators. If the stream connects and yields chunks, but the network silently drops or the provider's backend hangs mid-stream without terminating the connection, the native stream lacks an *idle read* timeout.
- The Result: The `iterator.next()` call waits forever for the next chunk, wedging the agent.

Reproduction Guide
If you'd like to see the tool-hanging scenario in action on the current `main` branch, you can register this mock tool:
```typescript
// Define a tool with a promise that never resolves
const hangingTool = {
  name: "hanging_tool",
  description: "A tool that simulates a hung subprocess.",
  execute: async () => {
    return new Promise(() => {}); // Hangs forever
  }
};
// Once the agent invokes this tool, the Pi UI will lock up indefinitely.
How this PR fixes it
If you check the included agent-loop.test.ts file in this PR, you will see a unit test specifically reproducing the streaming hang.

This patch introduces a strict boundary by wrapping both iterator.next() and tool.execute() in Promise.race handlers. This ensures that no matter what the LLM SDK or external tool does, the loop is guaranteed to either advance or gracefully throw a timeout error, allowing the application to recover. Let me know if you'd like me to tweak the default timeout values!

Fresh real-world repro on **v0.79.8** (this issue is filed against 0.74.2, so the behavior is still present), in case it helps narrow the boundaries — though what I hit is an adjacent variant rather than the exact mid-`execute()` wedge described here.

**Setup:** `pi -p` print mode, `ollama` provider (`llama3.2:3b`; same with a 14B and a 35B), one extension loaded (`pi-permission-system`). An external supervisor spawns one `pi -p --session-id <id> -p "<prompt>"` per request with its own 900s kill-timeout.

**Observed:** the turn *completes* — the assistant message is generated and written to the session `.jsonl` within ~10s — but the process never exits, and is then `SIGKILL`ed by the supervisor at 900000ms. One concrete trace:
- assistant reply persisted to the session at `00:39:38Z`
- supervisor logged `pi timed out after 900000ms` at `00:54:27Z` (+15:00 exactly)

Because the supervisor treats the kill as a failure, the already-generated reply is discarded and never delivered.

So this is the **post-completion non-exit** class, not the mid-execution wedge: the agent loop finishes cleanly, but the process won't return to the shell (same family as #2677 — no `process.exit()` after `runPrintMode()` when something keeps the event loop alive).

One detail that may help narrow it: with the **same extension loaded**, a *fresh* session drained and exited cleanly in ~30s (3/3 runs); the hang only reproduced when **resuming an established session** — there it was 100% reproducible, matching what was happening in production. So in this configuration the trigger was *session resume + extension loaded*, not extension presence alone.

The proposed `streamTimeoutMs` / `toolTimeoutMs` boundaries would catch the mid-execution class but not this one. For the non-exit case the missing piece is a hard `process.exit(exitCode)` after print mode (or unref-ing the lingering handles). Worth fixing alongside, since the user-visible symptom is identical: `pi -p` produces nothing and hangs until killed.
`pi -p` will hang if an extension does not shut down its resources in `session_end`.  This is expected.  Might be that this is a bug with the `pi-permission-system` extension or somethign similar.

Hi @mitsuhiko,

Just following up—I completely agree with you! Extensions absolutely should be well-behaved and clean up their resources (like pi-permission-system shutting down timers) in session_end.

However, the reality is that in "single-shot" supervisor environments or CI/CD pipelines where users rely on pi -p (print mode), the determinism of the process exiting cleanly is paramount. When runPrintMode() completes its job and restores stdout, the fact that a poorly behaved third-party extension can hold the entire pi process hostage from exiting means supervisors are forced to wait for a massive 900s SIGKILL timeout. By adding a simple process.exit(exitCode) at the very end of runPrintMode, we make the CLI bulletproof against any and all leaky extensions without breaking interactive mode.

We have actually taken this a step further. We've built an entire Pi Agent Improvement Suite to complement these core fixes, all backed by extensive unit and integration tests (which you can review in our repo here: [Paramveersingh-S/fluffy-harness](https://github.com/Paramveersingh-S/fluffy-harness)).

Here is what we've built and tested:

1. The Upstream Core Patch (upstream-pr/)

Added Promise.race() to the assistant stream iterator (agent-loop.ts) and tool executions to prevent mid-execution hangs. Includes the agent-loop.test.ts regression tests.
Added the strict process.exit(exitCode) to packages/coding-agent/src/main.ts for the print-mode fix.
2. pi-watchdog (Userspace Mitigation)

For users stuck on older versions of pi-agent-core before this patch merges, we built a userspace extension that actively tracks in-flight tools and stream delays, surfacing ctx.ui.notify warnings if either stalls for >60 seconds. We've included isolated mock tests in test/index.test.ts verifying the dual-notification system.
3. pi-bridge (General MCP Integration)

We built native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for the ecosystem! It translates MCP JSON Schema into Pi's native TypeBox representations, dynamically proxies executions over StdioClientTransport, and cleanly tears down child processes on session_shutdown. This is also heavily tested in test/integration.test.ts.
Let me know if you have any feedback on the upstream patch—we've tested it heavily against all our edge cases and it works perfectly!
